dark.name: InterviewQuestionPlayground
dark.text: Interview: the scoreboard that never fails The scoreboard has never failed, yet the waveform shows the DUT driving x on rdata after reset. The monitor copies vif.rdata into a bit [7:0] field named rdata, and the checker does if (rdata != exp) err++; What is the most complete explanation? != returns 1 when either operand holds x, so each error is counted, but the scoreboard's summary then filters those counts out. Simulators optimize x away in testbench code by default, so the fix is to enable the simulator's X-propagation mode. The bit copy turns x into 0, and a logic copy alone would not help either, because != returns x and the if then takes else. The DUT needs a default branch in its case statement; once that is added, the testbench as written will catch the bug. Submit answer

dark.name: InterviewQuestionPlayground
dark.text: Interview: one bit, one driver In one module, logic [1:0] v; is driven by assign v[0] = a; and assign v[1] = b; Is this legal? No: a variable may have only one continuous assignment in total, whichever bits it writes. Yes: each bit of a packed variable is an independent element, so each bit may have one continuous driver. Yes, and v resolves like a wire if a and b ever drive the same bit with different values. Only if v is declared bit [1:0] instead of logic [1:0], because bit has no x to resolve. Submit answer

Both are nets, because ports are always nets. a is a variable and y is a net. a is a net (input wire logic) and y is a variable. Submit answer

dark.name: InterviewQuestionPlayground
dark.text: Interview: an initializer is not an assign At module scope someone writes logic y = a & b; and expects y to follow a and b. What does y actually do when a changes later? Nothing: the declaration assignment initializes y once, before any initial or always procedure starts, and is not a continuous assignment. y follows a & b, exactly like wire y = a & b; because both declarations use the same assignment syntax. It does not compile: variables cannot have initializers at module scope, only inside procedures. y follows a & b in simulation, but synthesis ignores the initializer and leaves y undriven. light.name: InterviewQuestionPlayground
light.text: Interview: the scoreboard that never fails The scoreboard has never failed, yet the waveform shows the DUT driving x on rdata after reset. The monitor copies vif.rdata into a bit [7:0] field named rdata, and the checker does if (rdata != exp) err++; What is the most complete explanation? != returns 1 when either operand holds x, so each error is counted, but the scoreboard's summary then filters those counts out. Simulators optimize x away in testbench code by default, so the fix is to enable the simulator's X-propagation mode. The bit copy turns x into 0, and a logic copy alone would not help either, because != returns x and the if then takes else. The DUT needs a default branch in its case statement; once that is added, the testbench as written will catch the bug. Submit answer

light.name: InterviewQuestionPlayground
light.text: Interview: one bit, one driver In one module, logic [1:0] v; is driven by assign v[0] = a; and assign v[1] = b; Is this legal? No: a variable may have only one continuous assignment in total, whichever bits it writes. Yes: each bit of a packed variable is an independent element, so each bit may have one continuous driver. Yes, and v resolves like a wire if a and b ever drive the same bit with different values. Only if v is declared bit [1:0] instead of logic [1:0], because bit has no x to resolve. Submit answer

light.name: InterviewQuestionPlayground
light.text: Interview: an initializer is not an assign At module scope someone writes logic y = a & b; and expects y to follow a and b. What does y actually do when a changes later? Nothing: the declaration assignment initializes y once, before any initial or always procedure starts, and is not a continuous assignment. y follows a & b, exactly like wire y = a & b; because both declarations use the same assignment syntax. It does not compile: variables cannot have initializers at module scope, only inside procedures. y follows a & b in simulation, but synthesis ignores the initializer and leaves y undriven.
